# Case atlas, glossary and transfer {#sec-b28}





::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance

**Guiding question:** From which decision do I find the right method again?

**For:** everyone who starts a new project with this book, course participants at the start and the end of the
course, supervisors who assign a project · **Prerequisites:** none; the chapter is an entry point and points to the
chapters that hold the prerequisites

**In the course:** [W1 · From clinical case to question](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w1-from-clinical-case-to-question.html)
· [W8 · Colloquium and decision](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html)
(required) · **Data:** no patient data; the atlas, navigator and glossary are stored as tables in the chapter ·
**Core reading time:** about 9 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b28-case}

A newly appointed research coordinator in a fictitious trauma department receives three requests in her first week.
The rehabilitation team wants to check gait after ankle fractures with tablet videos. A laboratory group asks whether
it may publish hundreds of spectra from six animals as "a large dataset". The operating theatre manager wants to know
whether a second weekend team is worth the cost. She has two days to send each group a first answer: which question
they are really asking, which chapter they should read first, and which risk they must rule out before anyone writes
code. If she routes the requests by data type alone, the gait group starts with image processing and the laboratory
with model choice; both would miss the problem that decides their project.

## Core reading {#sec-b28-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W8 (and a first orientation in W1) · about 9 minutes · ends before 'Lab'
:::

### Start from the decision, not from the data

This chapter is the index of the book, organised by decisions. Most projects arrive with a data type – images,
spectra, a registry – and a method someone has heard of. The data type is a poor guide. A tablet video can serve a
method comparison (@sec-b11), a privacy assessment (@sec-b23) or a safety pilot (@sec-b20), and each needs a
different first step. **The key assumption of this chapter is that a method is found again through the decision it
supports and the risk that threatens it, not through the data it uses.** The data type narrows the choice; the
decision and the risk make it.

The chapter offers three tools for this. The *navigator* gives three entry routes to the 28 chapters: by goal, by data
type and by risk. The *case atlas* contains six new project vignettes, from a fracture alert to operating capacity.
Each one shows how a request turns into a target statement, a first test and a path through the chapters. The
*glossary* translates the book's terms between English and German, so that a reader can recognise a term from
clinical practice and find the chapter where it is introduced. A register of common mistakes and a one-page sketch for
the next experiment close the chapter. Its tables are stored as data in the chapter source, and the Lab checks that
every route points to an existing chapter.

### The route by risk

The risk route is the fastest when something has already gone wrong or is about to (@tbl-b28-risk). Each row names a
risk, the chapters that address it and the workshops in which it is practised. The first chapter in each row is the
one to open first.


::: {#tbl-b28-risk .cell tbl-cap='Navigator by risk. Each row leads from a risk to the chapters that address it, in the order in which they are best read, and to the workshops of the course. Unit: risk; no data.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Risk                                                   |Chapters (read the first one first)              |Workshops  |
|:------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:----------|
|A faulty or harmful alarm, too many false alarms       |@sec-b20, @sec-b27, @sec-b21, @sec-b09, @sec-b06 |W3, W7, W8 |
|Leakage between training and test in grouped data      |@sec-b19, @sec-b05, @sec-b27                     |W4         |
|Wrong n: repeated measurements counted as independent  |@sec-b03, @sec-b16, @sec-b10                     |W1, W4     |
|Poor calibration in a new setting                      |@sec-b06, @sec-b19                               |W3         |
|Selection or collider bias                             |@sec-b02                                         |W5         |
|Clusters that are artefacts of scaling or segmentation |@sec-b14, @sec-b12                               |W5         |
|Unit errors and unidentifiable parameters              |@sec-b15                                         |W6         |
|Distribution shift after an update or a season         |@sec-b20, @sec-b17                               |W6, W7     |
|Errors that fall unequally on groups                   |@sec-b21, @sec-b06                               |W3, W8     |
|Unclear intended purpose or changed use                |@sec-b22                                         |W7         |
|Unlawful data flow or re-identification of rare groups |@sec-b23, @sec-b26                               |W7         |
|Data leak, wrong model version or outage               |@sec-b24, @sec-b25, @sec-b20                     |W7         |
|Instructions hidden in documents                       |@sec-b25                                         |W2, W7     |
|Overstated claim in an abstract                        |@sec-b27, @sec-b07                               |W8         |


:::
:::


### Two reading routes as examples

*A clinician after a faulty alarm.* An alert flagged a fracture that was not there, and the patient received an
unnecessary CT scan. The clinician wants to know who must be told and who decides whether the alert stays on. The risk
route "a faulty or harmful alarm" leads first to @sec-b20, where the monitoring plan names the escalation path, the
fallback procedure and the person who may stop the pilot. The decision sheet in @sec-b27 records that person, and
@sec-b27-faulty-alarm lists who acts next, in order; @sec-b21 helps to explain the event to the patient. The next
responsible role is therefore the pilot lead named in the decision sheet as allowed to stop – not the developer and
not the clinician who happened to see the alert.

*A doctoral researcher with grouped spectra.* Hundreds of spectra come from a handful of animals. The data route
"hyperspectral images and grouped spectra" leads to @sec-b10 for the measurement, to @sec-b19 for a split by animal
with an ID overlap of zero, and to @sec-b27 for the passport and the reporting path
(@tbl-b27-reporting-paths): ARRIVE 2.0 for the animal study, TRIPOD+AI items for the model. The fill-in templates in
[Methods in R: ARRIVE](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-reporting-arrive.html) and
[Methods in R: TRIPOD-AI](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-reporting-tripod-ai.html) complete the report.

### Combining routes: the coordinator's three requests

The routes work best in combination. For the gait request, the data route ("video, landmarks and joint angles")
offers @sec-b11 and @sec-b23, and the risk route ("unlawful data flow or re-identification") offers @sec-b23 and
@sec-b26. The chapter that appears in both, @sec-b23, is where the coordinator starts: before anyone compares
measurement methods, the team must know whether raw video may be stored at all and when it is deleted. For the
laboratory, the data route leads to the split by animal in @sec-b19; "a large dataset" of spectra from six animals is,
for any statement about new animals, a dataset of six. For the operating theatre, two goal rows compete: "forecast
demand" (@sec-b17) and "compare capacity scenarios" (@sec-b18). The decision is about staffing, so the simulation is
the main tool and the forecast supplies its arrival assumptions. In each case the first chapter is chosen by the
decision and the risk; the data type only narrows the list.

### Working with the atlas

Each vignette in the atlas follows the same form: the decision, the data and the independent unit, a first baseline,
the main risk, a first observable test, the path through the chapters and the matching workshops. Read the vignette
nearest to your own project, then write your own version in the same fields before you open any chapter. The formative
model answers are kept separate and folded away, so that the attempt comes first. They are not marking schemes; they
show what a complete first answer contains.

**Question for the workshop:** Choose the vignette nearest to your project (W1) or to the project you defended (W8).
Which field of your own brief differs most from the vignette, and which chapter does that difference send you to?

## Lab {#sec-b28-lab}

The navigator, the atlas, the glossary and the register of mistakes are data frames in the source of this chapter. The
Lab checks them in the same way that a passport is checked: every route must lead to an existing chapter, every atlas
case must point to at least two chapters and one workshop, and the glossary must cover the book.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Size of the tables
c(navigator_rows = nrow(navigator), atlas_cases = length(atlas),
  glossary_terms = nrow(glossary), mistakes = nrow(mistakes))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> navigator_rows    atlas_cases glossary_terms       mistakes 
#>             50              6             95             18
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
nav_ids  <- trimws(unlist(strsplit(navigator$chapters, ",")))
mis_ids  <- trimws(unlist(strsplit(mistakes$chapters, ",")))
atlas_ids <- unlist(lapply(atlas, `[[`, "path"))

stopifnot(
  length(atlas) == 6,
  all(sapply(atlas, function(a) length(a$path) >= 2 && length(a$ws) >= 1)),
  all(unlist(lapply(atlas, `[[`, "ws")) %in% workshops$id),
  all(c(nav_ids, mis_ids, atlas_ids, glossary$chapter) %in% chapter_ids),   # no dangling references
  nrow(glossary) >= 60, !anyDuplicated(tolower(glossary$term)),
  all(chapter_ids %in% nav_ids)                                              # every chapter reachable
)
```
:::


All 28 chapters are reachable from the navigator, and no route points to a chapter that does not exist. The two
reading routes of the Core reading can be tested as searches. The function returns the chapters of every navigator
row whose entry contains the search term, in order of first appearance.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
find_route <- function(term) {
  rows <- navigator[grepl(term, navigator$entry, ignore.case = TRUE), ]
  unique(trimws(unlist(strsplit(rows$chapters, ","))))
}
route_alarm   <- find_route("alarm")
route_spectra <- find_route("spectra")
route_alarm
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "b20" "b27" "b21" "b09" "b06"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
route_spectra
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "b10" "b19" "b27"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(route_alarm[1] == "b20", "b27" %in% route_alarm,
          all(c("b10", "b19", "b27") %in% route_spectra))
```
:::


The atlas map shows which chapters the six vignettes use and in which order (@fig-b28-atlas-map). Chapters that no
vignette touches are not unimportant; they are reached through the navigator.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggplot2)

map_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(atlas), function(v)
  data.frame(vignette = v, chapter = atlas[[v]]$path, step = seq_along(atlas[[v]]$path))))
map_df$chapter <- factor(toupper(map_df$chapter), levels = toupper(chapter_ids))
map_df$vignette <- factor(map_df$vignette, levels = rev(names(atlas)))
map_df$first <- ifelse(map_df$step == 1, "first chapter", "later chapter")

ggplot(map_df, aes(chapter, vignette)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = first), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = step), size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("first chapter" = unname(cdsr_colours["orange"]),
                               "later chapter" = unname(cdsr_colours["skyblue"])), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vignette", caption = "Paths as listed in the case atlas; numbers give the reading order.") +
  theme_cdsr(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank())

stopifnot(nrow(map_df) == length(atlas_ids))
```

## Counter-check {#sec-b28-countercheck}

The path of a vignette is not fixed by its data. It changes when the target statement changes. The function below adds
chapters to a path when the target population moves from animals to patients, and when a research result is meant to
be used in care. Before running it, predict which chapters vignette A2 (wound perfusion in a pig model) gains if its
target statement becomes "patients with soft-tissue wounds in a supervised clinical pilot".


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
extend_path <- function(v, population, deployment) {
  a <- atlas[[v]]
  extra <- character(0)
  if (a$population == "animals" && population == "patients")
    extra <- c(extra, "b19", "b21", "b23")            # species transfer, ethics, personal data
  if (deployment && !a$deployment)
    extra <- c(extra, "b22", "b20", "b24", "b25")     # purpose, pilot, security
  unique(c(a$path, extra))
}
a2_moved <- extend_path("A2", population = "patients", deployment = TRUE)
setdiff(a2_moved, atlas$A2$path)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "b21" "b23" "b22" "b20" "b24" "b25"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(all(c("b21", "b22", "b23", "b20") %in% a2_moved),
          length(setdiff(a2_moved, atlas$A2$path)) == 6)
```
:::


The pig study gains six chapters: ethics with patients, regulation, data protection, the pilot and both security
chapters. Species transfer (@sec-b19) was already on the path, now with a harder question – not new animals, but a
new species. The data type did not change at all. This is the key assumption of the chapter in one line of code.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b28-consequences}

**Patients.** A wrong route costs time, but a route that skips a risk costs more. The most frequent failure is to
treat a project as purely technical: the gait group that never asks where the raw video goes, the laboratory that never
asks what a result per spectrum means for the next animals. The risk route exists to make these questions visible
before anyone is affected.

**Responsibility.** The atlas does not replace the people who carry responsibility: the statistician for the analysis
plan, the data protection officer for the data flow, the ethics committee and the animal welfare body for the study,
the regulatory function for the intended purpose, and the clinical lead for the decision to use a tool. Every vignette
therefore ends with a decision that a named role must take (@sec-b27).

**Regulation, data protection and security.** These topics enter a path through the risk route and through the
counter-check above. A vignette that stays in research has fewer of them; the moment a result is meant to change care,
@sec-b22 to @sec-b25 join the path.

**Keeping the atlas current.** Chapter numbers are stable identifiers, but legal dates, guidelines and sister-book
anchors change. The edition notes record the state of each edition; the Lab of this chapter is the first test to
rerun after any change to the chapter list.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b28-lookup}

**Reviewer question:** For a project you are asked to review, which row of the risk navigator would you open first,
and does the project's own documentation answer the question of that row?

**Self-test:** A pharmacy team asks whether a forecast of antibiotic consumption on the trauma wards can be used to
order stock two weeks ahead, and whether a dashboard could later suggest switching patients to oral treatment. Which
vignette is nearest, which part of the request changes the path, and which chapters join it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The nearest vignette is A6: a forecast of demand with a planning decision (@sec-b17), checked by a rolling-origin
backtest against a seasonal naive baseline. The first request stays in that path. The second request is different in
kind: suggesting a treatment change for individual patients makes the dashboard a decision aid about patients. That
part of the request brings in @sec-b22 (intended purpose and possible medical device status), @sec-b23 (patient-level
data flow), @sec-b21 (who bears the harm of a wrong suggestion) and, before any use, @sec-b20 (pilot and stop
criterion). The two requests should become two projects with two passports.
:::

### Case atlas

The six vignettes are new cases, not repeats of the chapter examples. All institutions, numbers and data are
fictitious; where a number would be needed, it is marked *open*.

#### A1 · A second look at the wrist

A hand-surgery outpatient clinic considers an alert, evaluated in a large emergency department, that flags possible
scaphoid fractures on wrist radiographs. Many of its patients were referred after negative imaging elsewhere.

- **Decision:** should an alert trigger a second read by a hand surgeon, and who follows up a missed fracture?
- **Data and unit:** one radiograph examination per patient and episode; reference standard: follow-up imaging.
- **First baseline:** current practice, a second read only on clinical suspicion.
- **Main risk:** prevalence and case mix differ from the evaluation site, so predictive values do not transfer; alert
  fatigue.
- **First observable test:** recompute the 2 × 2 table at the clinic's prevalence (*open*: local prevalence), then a
  pilot in shadow mode with a stop criterion.
- **Chapter path:** @sec-b09 → @sec-b06 → @sec-b19 → @sec-b20 → @sec-b21 → @sec-b27
- **Workshops:** [W3 · Diagnostics, prediction and evidence](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w3-diagnostics-prediction-evidence.html) · [W8 · Colloquium and decision](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html)
- **Look further:** [CTTIR Courses: Diagnostic testing – Se, Sp, PPV, NPV, LR](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course1_foundations/labs/lab_week2_session3.html)

#### A2 · Perfusion in soft-tissue wounds

A translational group records hyperspectral images of experimental soft-tissue wounds in a fictitious pig model:
several images per wound, two wounds per animal, three time points.

- **Decision:** is a confirmatory experiment justified, and with how many animals?
- **Data and unit:** spectra nested in images, wounds and animals; the independent unit is the animal.
- **First baseline:** a simple spectral index with a threshold fixed in advance.
- **Main risk:** leakage between images of the same animal; illumination differences between sessions.
- **First observable test:** split by animal with an ID overlap of zero; counter-check with a changed illumination
  reference.
- **Chapter path:** @sec-b10 → @sec-b19 → @sec-b16 → @sec-b27
- **Workshops:** [W4 · Imaging, gait and tissue](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w4-imaging-gait-tissue.html) · [W8 · Colloquium and decision](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html)
- **Look further:** [Methods in R: ARRIVE – animal research](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-reporting-arrive.html)

#### A3 · Walking again after an ankle fracture

A rehabilitation team films patients walking along the corridor with a tablet; software estimates the knee angle.

- **Decision:** can the tablet angle replace the laboratory measurement for the discharge assessment?
- **Data and unit:** many steps per patient, two methods; the independent unit is the patient.
- **First baseline:** the laboratory measurement as reference; a tolerance fixed clinically in advance.
- **Main risk:** camera angle and occlusion; raw video that identifies patients and is kept longer than needed.
- **First observable test:** difference plot per patient against the tolerance; a data flow with a deletion point for
  the raw video.
- **Chapter path:** @sec-b11 → @sec-b03 → @sec-b23 → @sec-b26
- **Workshops:** [W4 · Imaging, gait and tissue](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w4-imaging-gait-tissue.html) · [W5 · Causality, trajectories and phenotypes](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w5-causality-trajectories-phenotypes.html)
- **Look further:** [CTTIR Courses: Kappa, ICC, Bland–Altman](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course2_regression/labs/lab_week4_session2.html)

#### A4 · A serum marker after spinal cord injury

A fictitious cohort has a serum marker measured at irregular times over twelve weeks after spinal cord injury. Patients
in the worst condition are transferred or die earlier and contribute fewer measurements.

- **Decision:** should the early slope of the marker enter the protocol of a prognostic study?
- **Data and unit:** repeated measurements per patient; time zero is the injury.
- **First baseline:** a per-patient summary (change from the first measurement) next to a mixed model.
- **Main risk:** informative dropout; selection through intensive care admission.
- **First observable test:** sensitivity analysis for late measurements; a DAG for the selection step.
- **Chapter path:** @sec-b02 → @sec-b03 → @sec-b13 → @sec-b16
- **Workshops:** [W5 · Causality, trajectories and phenotypes](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w5-causality-trajectories-phenotypes.html)
- **Look further:** [CTTIR Courses: Linear mixed models with lme4](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course3_design_causal/labs/lab_week2_session3.html)

#### A5 · Cell types in a fracture callus

Multiplex-stained sections from fictitious fracture callus biopsies are segmented, and the resulting clusters are
labelled as new cell subtypes for a grant proposal.

- **Decision:** may the subtype label appear in the proposal as a finding?
- **Data and unit:** cells within sections within patients; the independent unit is the patient.
- **First baseline:** marker thresholds set by an expert (manual gating).
- **Main risk:** segmentation boundary, batch effects between staining runs, clusters produced by scaling; rare
  marker combinations in shared images.
- **First observable test:** shift the segmentation boundary and repeat the clustering on bootstrap samples; summarise
  per patient.
- **Chapter path:** @sec-b12 → @sec-b14 → @sec-b26 → @sec-b27
- **Workshops:** [W4 · Imaging, gait and tissue](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w4-imaging-gait-tissue.html) · [W5 · Causality, trajectories and phenotypes](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w5-causality-trajectories-phenotypes.html)
- **Look further:** [CTTIR Courses: Clustering – k-means, hierarchical, model-based](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course4_ml_highdim/labs/lab_week1_session4.html)

#### A6 · Weekend peaks in the trauma theatre

A fictitious trauma service sees more emergency operations at weekends. Management asks whether a second weekend team
would shorten the wait for hip fracture surgery.

- **Decision:** staff a second weekend team or not.
- **Data and unit:** daily arrivals for the forecast; waiting time per patient for the simulation.
- **First baseline:** a seasonal naive forecast; the current one-team scenario.
- **Main risk:** using a forecast to answer a capacity question; longer waits shifted onto lower-priority patients.
- **First observable test:** rolling-origin backtest of arrivals; both scenarios simulated on identical arrival
  streams, with the spread across runs.
- **Chapter path:** @sec-b17 → @sec-b18 → @sec-b20 → @sec-b21
- **Workshops:** [W6 · Pharmacometrics, forecasting and simulation](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w6-pharmacometrics-forecasting-simulation.html) · [W8 · Colloquium and decision](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html)
- **Look further:** [Methods in R: Rolling-origin cross-validation](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-09-timeseries.html#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-rolling-origin-cv)

### Formative model answers

Try your own brief first. Each answer names the target statement, the first test with its expected result and the
decision that a named role has to take.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Model answer A1"}
Target statement: "In patients referred to this clinic after a wrist injury, an alert-triggered second read finds
scaphoid fractures that would otherwise be missed, at an acceptable number of extra reads." First test: the 2 × 2 table
at the local prevalence, with the number of alerts per week as the workload measure. Expected result: a lower positive
predictive value than at the evaluation site if the local prevalence is lower – this alone is not a reason to reject
the tool. Decision: the clinic lead approves a shadow pilot and names who may stop it (@sec-b20, @sec-b27).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Model answer A2"}
Target statement: "In new pigs of the same strain, the index separates well from poorly perfused wound tissue." First
test: split by animal, ID overlap zero, result reported per animal with its interval. Expected result: a wide interval
with few animals; the passport then states which sample size the next experiment needs, justified with @sec-b16.
Decision: the principal investigator, with the animal welfare officer, decides whether the confirmatory experiment is
justified under the 3Rs.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Model answer A3"}
Target statement: "For patients after ankle fracture, the tablet angle agrees with the laboratory angle within the
clinical tolerance." First test: limits of agreement from per-patient means, compared with the tolerance fixed in
advance. Expected result: either agreement within tolerance or a systematic offset that depends on camera position.
Decision: the rehabilitation lead decides on use; the data protection officer approves the data flow and the deletion
point for raw video (@sec-b23).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Model answer A4"}
Target statement: "In patients after spinal cord injury, the marker slope over the first weeks is associated with the
later outcome." First test: mixed model against per-patient summaries, plus an analysis that assumes worse values for
patients who drop out. Expected result: if the slope changes materially under this assumption, the protocol must plan
for dropout. Decision: the study steering group decides whether the marker enters the protocol as a candidate, not as
a proven predictor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Model answer A5"}
Target statement: "Across patients, a cell population with this marker profile is reproducibly present in fracture
callus." First test: clustering repeated after shifting the segmentation boundary and on bootstrap samples, summarised
per patient. Expected result: a stable population is found again; an unstable one is reported as a hypothesis. Decision:
the principal investigator words the proposal accordingly; shared images are checked for rare combinations before
release (@sec-b26).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Model answer A6"}
Target statement: "Under the stated arrival assumptions, a second weekend team reduces the waiting time for hip
fracture surgery by an amount that justifies its cost." First test: forecast checked by backtest; both scenarios
simulated on identical arrival streams with the spread over runs. Expected result: a difference with a range, plus the
effect on lower-priority patients. Decision: the hospital management decides on staffing; the simulation report names
its assumptions (STRESS, @sec-b27).
:::

### Register of common mistakes

The register lists mistakes in reasoning and design, each with a warning sign and a check. Errors in software and
builds (packages, Quarto, renv, Git) are collected in
[Methods in R: Common errors](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-appendices-c-common-errors.html) and
[CTTIR Courses: Common errors](https://cttir.github.io/courses/appendices/common_errors.html). Four publications show
how widespread some of these mistakes are: leakage in machine-learning-based science [@kapoor2023leakage], the wrong
experimental unit in animal studies, where about half of the surveyed studies showed pseudoreplication
[*published*, @lazic2018n], neglected calibration [@vancalster2019calibration], and methodological flaws that left none
of 62 reviewed imaging models fit for clinical use [*published*, @roberts2021pitfalls].


::: {#tbl-b28-mistakes .cell tbl-cap='Register of common mistakes in reasoning and design. Unit: mistake; no data.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Mistake                                                 |Warning sign                                                      |Check                                                       |Chapters           |
|:-------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:------------------|
|Accuracy per image or spectrum, claim about individuals |n in the abstract exceeds the number of animals or patients       |ID overlap between training and test; result per individual |@sec-b19, @sec-b27 |
|Repeated measurements counted as independent            |narrow intervals from many measurements of few individuals        |name the experimental unit before the analysis              |@sec-b03, @sec-b16 |
|Predictive values carried into another setting          |same PPV quoted for a different prevalence                        |recompute the 2 × 2 table at the local prevalence           |@sec-b09           |
|Good ranking read as good calibration                   |only the AUC is reported                                          |calibration plot, observed against expected                 |@sec-b06           |
|Tuning or preprocessing on all data                     |test performance better than plausible                            |nested validation; preprocessing inside the folds           |@sec-b05           |
|Adjusting for a collider                                |association appears after restricting to admitted patients        |draw the DAG before modelling                               |@sec-b02           |
|Clusters read as subtypes                               |clusters change with scaling, seed or segmentation                |stability check and alternative scaling                     |@sec-b14, @sec-b12 |
|Unit error in a mechanistic model                       |implausible clearance or volume                                   |units carried through; analytic solution as check           |@sec-b15           |
|Forecast interval read as a guarantee                   |coverage never checked on later data                              |rolling-origin backtest with coverage                       |@sec-b17           |
|Unverified simulation                                   |no trace of single entities, different input streams per scenario |event log of one entity; identical arrival streams          |@sec-b18           |
|Pilot without a stop criterion                          |no denominator, no named person, no date                          |monitoring plan with escalation and stop rule               |@sec-b20, @sec-b27 |
|Research label taken as legal basis                     |no documented legal basis for the change of purpose               |legal basis per purpose; data protection officer            |@sec-b23, @sec-b26 |
|Pseudonymised data taken as anonymous                   |key exists; rare combinations in the release                      |k-anonymity check; assessment per recipient                 |@sec-b26           |
|Trusting the model to ignore embedded instructions      |assistant can act on document content                             |permission tests with synthetic documents                   |@sec-b25           |
|Version label trusted instead of checksum               |same version, different behaviour                                 |compare checksum with the release record                    |@sec-b24, @sec-b25 |
|Fabricated or misattributed citation                    |reference not found or passage does not support the claim         |check DOI, title and the cited passage                      |@sec-b08           |
|Use drifts beyond the intended purpose                  |tool used for decisions it was not meant for                      |compare actual use with the stated purpose                  |@sec-b22           |
|Speed claim without benchmark                           |one language is called faster                                     |benchmark on identical inputs and tolerance                 |@sec-b15           |

### The next experiment on one page

Every project ends with a next step, and the next step is best written down before the colloquium. The sketch below
fits on one page. The right-hand column shows it filled in for vignette A2; the same form works for a security test,
for example a rerun of the control matrix of @sec-b25 after a model update.

| Field | Next validation experiment for A2 (example) |
|---|---|
| Target statement | Spectral index separates well from poorly perfused wound tissue in new pigs of the same strain |
| What would change the decision | Agreement per animal above the threshold fixed in advance → confirmatory study; below → stop and revise the index |
| Design | New animals only; split by animal; same device, protocol and illumination reference as before |
| Independent unit and n | Animal; n justified in advance with a prior from the pilot (@sec-b16) – *open* until calculated |
| Baseline and comparator | The fixed index from the pilot; the reference rule of @sec-b27 as a floor |
| Primary measure with denominator | Correct classification per animal, with exact interval |
| Counter-check | Changed illumination reference in a subset of sessions |
| Pre-registration and stop criterion | Analysis plan filed before the first animal; stop if the interim check shows the index fails in both classes |
| Roles | Principal investigator (decision), statistician (analysis plan), animal welfare officer (3Rs) |
| Risks and controls | Ethics: animal numbers; data: checksum of the analysis script; no personal data |
| Review date | After the analysis plan is approved; date set by the principal investigator |

**Annotated sources**

- @kapoor2023leakage – survey of data leakage across 17 fields of machine-learning-based science, with a taxonomy of
  eight leakage types; background for the first row of the register.
- @lazic2018n – survey of animal experiments showing how often the experimental unit is chosen wrongly.
- @vancalster2019calibration – why calibration, not only discrimination, decides whether predictions can be used.
- @roberts2021pitfalls – systematic review of imaging models with a list of recurring methodological pitfalls.
